title: PRACTICE SET 1
focus: Focus: Import/export, bar chart & boxplot, dplyr basics
info: Total: 25 marks  |  Suggested time: 1 hour  |  Answer ALL questions. Write all R code by hand.

subquestions.text: A committee member of the Gerbang Malam night market has recorded a stall survey in a file named market_survey.csv. Write the base R command to import this file into R and store it in a variable named market_data.
subquestions.reference_answer: market_data <- read.csv("market_survey.csv")

subquestions.text: Write the R code to import the second sheet of an Excel file named stall_list.xlsx using the readxl package.
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(readxl)
read_excel("stall_list.xlsx", sheet = 2)

subquestions.text: Write the base R command to export a data frame named clean_data to a CSV file named market_clean.csv without row numbers.
subquestions.reference_answer:
write.csv(clean_data, "market_clean.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)

questions.context: Assume a dataset pasar_data has been imported into RStudio. It contains the numeric variable Daily_Sales (RM) and the factor variables Stall_Category (“Food” / “Clothes” / “Toys”) and Day_Type (“Weekday” / “Weekend”). Use the ggplot2 package for all plots.

subquestions.text: Write the R code to create a bar chart showing the number of stalls in each Stall_Category, with a main title, axis labels, and orange bars.
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(pasar_data, aes(x = Stall_Category)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Number of Stalls by Category",
       x = "Stall Category", y = "Number of Stalls")

subquestions.text: Write the R code to create a boxplot of Daily_Sales across the two categories of Day_Type.
subquestions.reference_answer:
ggplot(pasar_data,
  aes(x = Day_Type, y = Daily_Sales)) +
  geom_boxplot()

subquestions.text:
The boxplot below was produced from the pasar_data dataset.
State the approximate median daily sales for each day type, and state which day type shows the larger spread in daily sales.
subquestions.reference_answer:
Median for Weekday ≈ RM500 (accept ±RM30)
Median for Weekend ≈ RM900 (accept ±RM30)
Larger spread: Weekend (wider box / longer whiskers)

questions.context:
The dataset stall_data records the performance of five stalls:
Use the dplyr package and the pipe operator (%>%) for all parts.

subquestions.text: Select the Stall and Daily_Sales variables and filter the stalls with Daily_Sales more than 700. Store the result as top_stalls. Your output should be:
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(dplyr)
top_stalls <- stall_data %>%
  select(Stall, Daily_Sales) %>%
  filter(Daily_Sales > 700)

subquestions.text: Arrange all stalls by Daily_Sales in descending order. Store the result as sales_rank.
subquestions.reference_answer:
sales_rank <- stall_data %>%
  arrange(desc(Daily_Sales))

subquestions.text: Use mutate() to create a new variable Profit, defined as Profit = Daily_Sales − Cost.
subquestions.reference_answer:
stall_data <- stall_data %>%
  mutate(Profit = Daily_Sales - Cost)

subquestions.text:
Continuing from c), use group_by() and summarise() to compute the average Profit for each Category, naming the column Avg_Profit. Store the result as category_summary.
END OF PRACTICE SET
subquestions.reference_answer:
category_summary <- stall_data %>%
  group_by(Category) %>%
  summarise(Avg_Profit = mean(Profit))

subquestions.text: Perak Transit has recorded commuter survey data in an SPSS file named commuter.sav. Write the R code to import this file using the haven package and store it in a variable named commuter_data.
subquestions.reference_answer:

subquestions.reference_answer:

subquestions.text: Besides CSV and SPSS, state TWO (2) other file formats that can be imported into R.
subquestions.reference_answer: Any two: Excel (.xlsx/.xls), Stata (.dta), text/tab-delimited (.txt), JSON (.json), SAS (.sas7bdat)

questions.context: Assume a dataset monthly_riders has been imported into RStudio, containing the variables Month (numbers 1 to 12) and Passengers. A second dataset, trip_data, contains the factor variables Route (“A” / “B” / “C”) and Ticket_Type (“Adult” / “Student”). Use the ggplot2 package for all plots.

subquestions.text: Using monthly_riders, write the R code to create a line chart of Passengers across Month, with a main title, axis labels, and a green line.
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(monthly_riders, aes(x = Month, y = Passengers)) +
  geom_line(color = "green") +
  labs(title = "Monthly Passengers",
       x = "Month", y = "Number of Passengers")

subquestions.text: Using trip_data, write the R code to create a stacked bar chart of Route, where each bar is divided (filled) according to Ticket_Type.
subquestions.reference_answer:
ggplot(trip_data,
  aes(x = Route, fill = Ticket_Type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack")
(geom_bar() alone is accepted – “stack” is the default)

subquestions.text: Explain the difference in output between using position = “stack” and position = “dodge” in geom_bar(), and state which one is more suitable if the manager wants to compare Adult vs Student tickets directly side by side.
subquestions.reference_answer:
"stack" – the segments are placed on top of one another in a single bar for each route (shows the total).
"dodge" – the bars are placed side by side within each route.
For a direct side-by-side comparison of Adult vs Student, position = "dodge" is more suitable.

questions.context: The dataset bus_data records weekly information for five routes:

subquestions.text: State the output that R will return if mean(bus_data$Passengers) is executed without handling the NA values, and explain why.
subquestions.reference_answer: It returns NA, because any arithmetic calculation involving NA produces NA.

subquestions.text: Write an R script to compute the average number of passengers, ensuring that the NA values are excluded.
subquestions.reference_answer: mean(bus_data$Passengers, na.rm = TRUE)

subquestions.text: Using dplyr and the pipe operator, rename the variable Complaints to Feedback_Count. Store the result as bus_renamed.
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(dplyr)
bus_renamed <- bus_data %>%
  rename(Feedback_Count = Complaints)

subquestions.text: Using dplyr and the pipe operator, select the Route and Passengers variables and filter the routes with more than 400 passengers. Store the result as busy_routes.
subquestions.reference_answer:
busy_routes <- bus_data %>%
  select(Route, Passengers) %>%
  filter(Passengers > 400)
(Rows with NA in Passengers are automatically dropped by filter)

subquestions.text:
Using dplyr and the pipe operator, arrange all routes by Passengers in descending order. Store the result as route_rank.
END OF PRACTICE SET
subquestions.reference_answer:
route_rank <- bus_data %>%
  arrange(desc(Passengers))

subquestions.text: Bakeri Hangat keeps its oven production log in a text file named oven_log.txt, in which the values are separated by semicolons (;) and the first row contains the variable names. Write the base R command to import this file into a variable named oven_data.
subquestions.reference_answer:
oven_data <- read.table("oven_log.txt",
             header = TRUE, sep = ";")

subquestions.text: State the purpose of the argument header = TRUE in the command written in a).
subquestions.reference_answer: It tells R that the first row of the file contains the variable (column) names, so it is not treated as data.

subquestions.text: Write the base R command to export a data frame named daily_report to a CSV file named report_today.csv without row numbers.

          row.names = FALSE)

questions.context: Assume a dataset sales_daily has been imported into RStudio. It contains the numeric variable Items_Sold and the factor variables Branch (“Ipoh” / “Taiping”) and Shift (“Morning” / “Evening”). Use the ggplot2 package for all plots.

subquestions.text: Write the R code to create a histogram of Items_Sold using a bin width of 5, with a main title, axis labels, and brown bars.
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(sales_daily, aes(x = Items_Sold)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "brown") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Items Sold per Day",
       x = "Items Sold", y = "Frequency")

subquestions.text: Write the R code to create a clustered (grouped) bar chart of Branch, where the bars for the two shifts appear side by side within each branch.
subquestions.reference_answer:
ggplot(sales_daily,
  aes(x = Branch, fill = Shift)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")

subquestions.text:
The histogram below was produced from the sales_daily dataset.
Describe the shape of the distribution, state the class interval with the highest frequency, and state whether the mean is greater than, less than, or equal to the median.
subquestions.reference_answer:
Shape: skewed to the left (negatively skewed).
Highest frequency: the 40–45 class.
The mean is less than the median (the mean is pulled towards the long left tail).

questions.context: The dataset bakery_data records yesterday's performance of five products:

subquestions.text: Write an R command using is.na() to count the number of missing values in the Waste column, and state the value it returns for this dataset.
subquestions.reference_answer:
sum(is.na(bakery_data$Waste))
It returns 2.

subquestions.text: Explain what happens to the dataset if na.omit(bakery_data) is applied. In your answer, state which items remain and give one reason why this may be a problem.
subquestions.reference_answer:
na.omit() removes every row that contains at least one NA.
Only Baguette, Donut and Muffin remain (Croissant and Roti are removed).
Problem: complete information about Sold, Price and Revenue for Croissant and Roti is also lost, even though only their Waste values were missing.

subquestions.text: Using dplyr and the pipe operator, use mutate() to create a new variable Revenue, defined as Revenue = Sold × Price_RM.
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(dplyr)
bakery_data <- bakery_data %>%
  mutate(Revenue = Sold * Price_RM)

subquestions.text:
Continuing from c), use group_by() and summarise() to compute the total Sold for each Type, naming the column Total_Sold. Store the result as type_summary.
END OF PRACTICE SET
subquestions.reference_answer:
type_summary <- bakery_data %>%
  group_by(Type) %>%
  summarise(Total_Sold = sum(Sold))

title: PRACTICE SET 4

subquestions.text: State ONE (1) difference between the base R function read.csv() and the readr function read_csv().
subquestions.reference_answer:
Any one (2 marks):
1. read.csv() is base R (no package), read_csv() requires the readr package.
2. read_csv() is faster for large files.
3. read_csv() returns a tibble; read.csv() returns a data frame.
4. read_csv() does not automatically convert strings to factors.

questions.context:

Use the dplyr package and the pipe operator (%>%) for all parts.

subquestions.text: Select the Model and Units_Sold variables and filter the models that sold 45 units or more. Store the result as hot_models. Your output should be:

questions.context: Assume a dataset futsal_data has been imported into RStudio. It contains the numeric variable Match_Rating (a score out of 10 given by referees) and the factor variables Team (“Falcons” / “Titans”) and Division (“A” / “B”). Use the ggplot2 package for all plots.

subquestions.text: Write the R code to create a bar chart showing the number of matches played in each Division.
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(futsal_data, aes(x = Division)) +
  geom_bar()

subquestions.text: Write the R code to create a boxplot of Match_Rating across the two teams, with a descriptive main title, appropriate axis labels, and a different colour for each team.
subquestions.reference_answer:
ggplot(futsal_data,
  aes(x = Team, y = Match_Rating, fill = Team)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Match Rating by Team",
       x = "Team", y = "Match Rating (out of 10)")

subquestions.text:
The boxplot below was produced from the futsal_data dataset.
State the approximate median match rating for each team, state which team is more consistent (smaller spread), and comment on any outlier shown.
subquestions.reference_answer:
Median for Falcons ≈ 7.5; median for Titans ≈ 6.0 (accept ±0.3)
More consistent: Falcons (much smaller box / shorter whiskers)
There is one outlier in the Falcons group – a very low rating of about 2, far below the rest of their ratings.

questions.context: The dataset player_stats records this season's statistics for five players:

subquestions.text: Write an R script to compute the average number of goals (Goals) using the mean() function, ensuring that the NA value is excluded.
subquestions.reference_answer: mean(player_stats$Goals, na.rm = TRUE)

subquestions.text: A teammate suggests replacing the NA in Goals with 0 before the analysis. Discuss whether this suggestion is appropriate.
subquestions.reference_answer:
Not appropriate. NA means the number of goals was not recorded – it does not mean the player scored 0 goals.
Replacing it with 0 would wrongly lower the averages and bias the analysis; it is better to exclude it with na.rm = TRUE or obtain the true value.

subquestions.text: Using dplyr and the pipe operator, use mutate() to create a new variable Goals_per_Match, defined as Goals_per_Match = Goals / Matches.
subquestions.reference_answer:
library(dplyr)
player_stats <- player_stats %>%
  mutate(Goals_per_Match = Goals / Matches)

subquestions.text:
Continuing from c), use group_by() and summarise() to compute the average Goals for each Team, naming the column Avg_Goals. Remember to handle the NA value inside the calculation. Store the result as team_summary.
END OF PRACTICE SET
subquestions.reference_answer:
team_summary <- player_stats %>%
  group_by(Team) %>%
  summarise(Avg_Goals = mean(Goals, na.rm = TRUE))
